text: Section 15 — Salaries [IT Act 1961, as amended up to Finance Act 2025] 15. The following incomes shall be chargeable to income-tax under the head "Salaries"— (a) any salary due from an employer or a former employer to an assessee in the previous year, whether paid or not; (b) any salary paid or allowed to him in the previous year by or on behalf of an employer or a former employer though not due or before it became due to him; (c) any arrears of salary paid or allowed to him in the previous year by or on behalf of an employer or a former employer, if not charged to income-tax for any earlier previous year. Explanation 1.—For the removal of doubts, it is hereby declared that where any salary paid before it became due is included in the total income of the assessee for the previous year in which it is paid, it shall not be included again in the total income of the assessee for the previous year in which the salary becomes due. Explanation 2.—For the purposes of this section, "salary" includes wages, any annuity or pension, any gratuity, any fees, commission, perquisite or profits in lieu of or in addition to any salary or wages, any advance of salary, any payment received in respect of any period of leave not availed of by him, and the annual accretion to the balance at the credit of an employee participating in a recognised provident fund, to the extent to which it is chargeable to tax under rule 6 of Part A of the Fourth Schedule, and the aggregate of all sums that are comprised in the transferred balance of an employee participating in a recognised provident fund, to the extent to which it is chargeable to tax under sub-rule (4) of rule 11 of Part A of the Fourth Schedule. Note: The full definition of "salary" is contained in Section 17 of the IT Act. Section 17(1) defines salary as including wages, annuity, pension, gratuity, fees, commissions, perquisites, profits in lieu of salary, leave encashment, and EPF

the Fourth Schedule. Note: The full definition of "salary" is contained in Section 17 of the IT Act. Section 17(1) defines salary as including wages, annuity, pension, gratuity, fees, commissions, perquisites, profits in lieu of salary, leave encashment, and EPF accretions. Section 17(2) defines perquisites. Section 17(3) defines profits in lieu of salary. All three sub-sections together constitute the comprehensive definition of taxable salary income for purposes of Section 15. Note on "due, paid, or allowed": - Salary "due" means earned in the previous year, regardless of when received. - Salary "paid" or "allowed" includes advance salary credited in the previous year. - Arrears of salary are included in the year of receipt, not the year to which they relate, unless already charged in a prior year. Relief for arrears of salary: Where salary arrears are taxable in the current year but relate to past years, relief may be claimed under Section 89(1) read with Rule 21A — allowing the assessee to recompute tax as if the arrears had been received in the respective earlier years and claim the differential as relief.

Section 16 — Deductions from salaries [IT Act 1961, as amended up to Finance Act 2025] 16. In computing the income chargeable under the head "Salaries", the following deductions shall be allowed, namely:— 16(i) Standard deduction: A deduction of a sum equal to fifty thousand rupees or the amount of salary, whichever is less, shall be allowed under this clause. [AY2025-26 Budget 2025 Note: For taxpayers opting for the new tax regime under Section 115BAC, the standard deduction has been enhanced to seventy-five thousand rupees effective Assessment Year 2025-26 (Financial Year 2024-25), by insertion of sub-section (2A) in Section 115BAC. The standard deduction under Section 16(i) for the old (regular) tax regime remains fifty thousand rupees.] 16(ii) Entertainment allowance: Any allowance in the nature of an entertainment allowance, not exceeding the least of— (a) one-fifth of the salary (exclusive of any allowance, benefit or other perquisite) of the employee, or (b) five thousand rupees, shall be deductible in the case of an employee of the Government (not of a company or of any other employer). In computing the income of an employee other than a Government employee, entertainment allowance is not deductible under this clause. Proviso to 16(ii): The deduction under clause (ii) shall be equal to the least of— (a) the amount of the allowance actually received by the assessee in the previous year in respect of the said period; or (b) one-fifth of his salary for the said period, excluding all allowances, benefits or other perquisites; or (c) five thousand rupees. This deduction is available ONLY to Government employees (Central Government and State Government). Private sector employees cannot claim entertainment allowance deduction. 16(iii) Tax on employment (professional tax): The tax on employment within the meaning of sub-clause (ii) of clause (24) of article 276 of the Constitution (hereinafter referred to as "professional tax"), leviable by or under any law, to the extent to which such tax is actually paid by the assessee, shall be deductible. Professional tax is a tax levied by State Governments under Article 276 of the Constitution of India. It is deductible in full —

law, to the extent to which such tax is actually paid by the assessee, shall be deductible. Professional tax is a tax levied by State Governments under Article 276 of the Constitution of India. It is deductible in full — the entire amount of professional tax paid during the previous year is deductible under Section 16(iii), without any ceiling. Note: Professional tax paid by the employer on behalf of the employee is first treated as a perquisite (taxable income) and then simultaneously allowed as a deduction under 16(iii), resulting in a net nil tax impact. Summary of Section 16 Deductions (for ITR-1 Schedule S): Field 7a — Standard deduction: ₹50,000 (old regime) or ₹75,000 (new regime, since AY 2025-26; applies to AY 2026-27) Field 7b — Entertainment allowance [Section 16(ii)]: Government employees only; limited to least of actual allowance, 1/5th of salary, or ₹5,000 Field 7c — Professional tax [Section 16(iii)]: Full amount paid by assessee during previous year Field 7d — Total deductions under Section 16: Sum of 7a + 7b + 7c

Section 10(13A) — HRA Exemption [IT Act 1961, as amended up to Finance Act 2025] 10. In computing the total income of a previous year of any person, any income falling within any of the following clauses shall not be included— 10(13A): any special allowance specifically granted to an assessee by his employer to meet expenditure actually incurred on payment of rent (by whatever name called) in respect of residential accommodation occupied by the assessee, to such extent as may be prescribed having regard to the area or place in which such accommodation is situate and other relevant considerations. Proviso to 10(13A): Nothing in this clause shall apply to any such allowance received by an assessee who— (a) owns any residential accommodation at the place at which he ordinarily resides or performs duties of his office or employment; or (b) does not actually incur expenditure on payment of rent (by whatever name called) in respect of the residential accommodation occupied by him. Explanation.— For the purposes of this clause, "prescribed" means prescribed by the rules made under this Act. [The extent of exemption is prescribed in Rule 2A of the Income Tax Rules, 1962. See the Rule 2A file for the min-of-3 computation formula.] Conditions for claiming 10(13A) exemption: 1. The assessee must be a salaried employee — self-employed individuals cannot claim HRA exemption. 2. The allowance must be specifically granted by the employer to meet rent expenditure (HRA component must appear in the salary structure). 3. The assessee must actually pay rent for residential accommodation. 4. The assessee must not own a residential house in the city where the duty is performed or where the residence is located. 5. If the assessee owns a house in a different city but rents accommodation in the place of employment, the exemption is still available. Computation of HRA Exemption (Rule 2A — min-of-3 formula): The exempt portion of HRA is the LEAST of the following three amounts: (a) Actual HRA received from employer (annual amount) (b) 50% of salary (basic + DA) for metro cities (Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai) OR 40% of

min-of-3 formula): The exempt portion of HRA is the LEAST of the following three amounts: (a) Actual HRA received from employer (annual amount) (b) 50% of salary (basic + DA) for metro cities (Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai) OR 40% of salary (basic + DA) for non-metro/other cities (c) Actual rent paid annually MINUS 10% of salary (basic + DA) The balance of HRA (received minus exempt) is taxable as part of salary. "Salary" for HRA purposes means: Basic Salary + Dearness Allowance forming part of salary for retirement benefits. Other allowances and perquisites are excluded. If the assessee does not pay any rent, no exemption is available — the entire HRA received is taxable. Rent receipts and landlord's PAN: If annual rent paid exceeds ₹1,00,000 (i.e., monthly rent > ₹8,333), the landlord's PAN must be furnished to the employer for the HRA exemption to be allowed by the employer in Form 16. ITR-1 Schedule S Field 5: HRA exemption under Section 10(13A) is reported as an exempt allowance in Field 5 (Allowances to the extent exempt under Section 10). The exempt HRA amount is deducted from gross salary to arrive at net salary.

Section 10(5) — LTA Exemption [IT Act 1961, as amended up to Finance Act 2025] 10. In computing the total income of a previous year of any person, any income falling within any of the following clauses shall not be included— 10(5): the value of any travel concession or assistance received by or due to an employee from his employer or former employer for himself and his family, in connection with his proceeding— (a) on leave to any place in India; (b) to any place in India after retirement from service or after the termination of his service, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed (including conditions as to number of journeys and the amount which shall be exempt per head) having regard to the travel by the shortest route to that place. Explanation.— For the purposes of this clause, "family", in relation to an individual, means— (i) the spouse and children of the individual; and (ii) the parents, brothers and sisters of the individual or any of them, wholly or mainly dependent on the individual. Prescribed Conditions (Rule 6B of Income Tax Rules, 1962): Block of 4 years: The Central Government notifies 4-year calendar blocks for LTA purposes. Current block: 2022–2025 (January 2022 to December 2025). Two journeys are permissible in each 4-year block. Number of journeys: An employee can claim LTA exemption for maximum 2 journeys within a 4-year block. If the employee does not claim exemption for 1 or both journeys in a block, the unclaimed journey(s) can be carried forward to the first calendar year of the immediately succeeding block (one carry-forward journey only). Qualifying travel: Travel must be within India only. International travel does not qualify. Travel must be for the purpose of leave — the employee must actually travel (not just receive a travel allowance without travelling). Mode of travel and limits: (a) Travel by air: Economy class airfare by the shortest route. If no air service, then as per (b) below. (b) Travel by rail: AC First Class rail fare by the shortest route (or actual if less than AC First Class).

Travel by air: Economy class airfare by the shortest route. If no air service, then as per (b) below. (b) Travel by rail: AC First Class rail fare by the shortest route (or actual if less than AC First Class). (c) Travel by any other mode to destinations not connected by rail or air: First class or deluxe class fare by the shortest route. Family coverage: The exemption covers the employee AND family members (as defined in the Explanation above). However, where the number of family members accompanying the employee exceeds 2 children born on or after 01-10-1998, the exemption for the excess children is NOT available (i.e., only 2 children born after 01-10-1998 qualify; children born before 01-10-1998 are not subject to this limit; twins or triplets in a single birth are treated as one child for this purpose). What is exempt: Only actual travel costs are exempt — hotel accommodation, sightseeing, local conveyance at the destination are not covered. The exemption is limited to the cost of travel to and from the destination by the eligible mode and class. Proof and employer claim: The exemption is available to employees who declare LTA travel to their employer. The employer may verify travel tickets and boarding passes. The excess (LTA received minus exempt portion) is taxable as salary. ITR-1 Schedule S Field 5: LTA exemption under Section 10(5) is included in Field 5 (Allowances exempt under Section 10) along with HRA and other exemptions.

Section 10(10D) — Life Insurance Maturity Proceeds [IT Act 1961, as amended up to Finance Act 2025] 10. In computing the total income of a previous year of any person, any income falling within any of the following clauses shall not be included— 10(10D): any sum received under a life insurance policy, including the sum allocated by way of bonus on such policy, other than— (a) any sum received under sub-section (3) of section 80DD or sub-section (3) of section 80DDA; or (b) any sum received under a Keyman insurance policy; or (c) any sum received under an insurance policy issued on or after the 1st day of April, 2003, in respect of which the premium payable for any of the years during the term of the policy exceeds twenty per cent of the actual capital sum assured; or (d) any sum received under an insurance policy issued on or after the 1st day of April, 2012, in respect of which the premium payable for any of the years during the term of the policy exceeds ten per cent of the actual capital sum assured: Provided that the provisions of sub-clauses (c) and (d) shall not apply to any sum received on the death of a person. Provided further that where the premium payable for any of the years during the term of a policy of insurance referred to in sub-clause (c) or sub-clause (d), issued on or after the 1st day of April, 2013, in respect of persons with disability or persons with severe disability as referred to in section 80U or suffering from disease or ailment as specified in the rules made under section 80DDB, exceeds fifteen per cent of the actual capital sum assured, the exemption under this clause shall not apply to such policy. [Finance Act 2021 Amendment — ULIPs issued on or after 01-02-2021]: (e) any sum received under a Unit Linked Insurance Plan (ULIP) issued on or after the 1st day of February, 2021, where the amount of premium payable for any of the previous years during the term of such policy exceeds two

any sum received under a Unit Linked Insurance Plan (ULIP) issued on or after the 1st day of February, 2021, where the amount of premium payable for any of the previous years during the term of such policy exceeds two lakh and fifty thousand rupees: Provided that where premium is payable by a person for more than one such ULIP issued on or after the 1st day of February, 2021, the exemption under this clause shall not apply with respect to such ULIP or ULIPs where the aggregate amount of premium exceeds two lakh and fifty thousand rupees in any previous year. Provided further that the provisions of this sub-clause shall not apply to any sum received on the death of a person. Explanation for 10(10D): (i) "Keyman insurance policy" means a life insurance policy taken by a person on the life of another person who is or was the employee of the first-mentioned person or is or was connected in any manner whatsoever with the business of the first-mentioned person. (ii) For the purposes of this clause, the expression "actual capital sum assured" in relation to a life insurance policy means the minimum amount assured under the policy on happening of the insured event at any time during the term of the policy, excluding— (a) the value of any premium agreed to be returned; or (b) any benefit by way of bonus or otherwise over and above the sum actually assured, which is to be or may be received under the policy by any person. Summary of 10(10D) Exemption with premium thresholds: - Policy issued BEFORE 01-04-2003: Maturity proceeds fully exempt (no premium cap) - Policy issued ON/AFTER 01-04-2003 but BEFORE 01-04-2012: Exempt only if annual premium ≤ 20% of sum assured - Policy issued ON/AFTER 01-04-2012: Exempt only if annual premium ≤ 10% of sum assured - ULIP issued ON/AFTER 01-02-2021: Exempt only if annual premium ≤ ₹2,50,000 - Disability/critical illness policies (post 01-04-2013): Exempt if premium ≤ 15% of sum assured - Death benefit: ALWAYS exempt regardless of premium percentage or ULIP cap Note: Policies where the

issued ON/AFTER 01-02-2021: Exempt only if annual premium ≤ ₹2,50,000 - Disability/critical illness policies (post 01-04-2013): Exempt if premium ≤ 15% of sum assured - Death benefit: ALWAYS exempt regardless of premium percentage or ULIP cap Note: Policies where the premium exceeds the applicable threshold do not get full exemption — the maturity proceeds become taxable (either under "Capital gains" for ULIP or "Income from other sources"). This makes Section 10(10D) exclusions a critical planning consideration for high-premium life insurance purchasers.

Section 24 — Deductions from income from house property [IT Act 1961, as amended up to Finance Act 2025] 24. Income chargeable under the head "Income from house property" shall be computed after making the following deductions, namely:— 24(a) Standard deduction: A sum equal to thirty per cent of the annual value. 24(b) Interest on borrowed capital: Where the property has been acquired, constructed, repaired, renewed or reconstructed with borrowed capital, the amount of any interest payable on such capital: Provided that in respect of property referred to in sub-section (2) of section 23 (i.e., self-occupied property), the amount of deduction shall not exceed— (A) two lakh rupees, if— (i) the property is acquired or constructed with capital borrowed on or after the 1st day of April, 1999; (ii) the acquisition or construction is completed within five years from the end of the financial year in which the capital was borrowed; and (iii) the assessee furnishes a certificate, from the person to whom any interest is payable on the capital borrowed, specifying the amount of interest payable by the assessee for the purpose of such acquisition or construction of the property; (B) thirty thousand rupees in any other case. Proviso to 24(b): According to sub-section (2) of section 23, where the property is used for self-occupation throughout the previous year, the annual value shall be taken to be nil. In such a case: - If capital is borrowed on or after 01-04-1999 AND construction is completed within 5 years from the end of the FY in which loan is taken, deduction limit is ₹2,00,000. - In any other case (e.g., loan taken before 01-04-1999, or construction not completed within 5 years), deduction limit is ₹30,000. Explanation.— Where the acquisition or construction of the house property is not completed within the period mentioned in sub-clause (ii) of clause (A) above, the deduction allowable shall be as per clause (B), i.e., ₹30,000 only. Pre-construction interest: Interest paid prior to the year in which the house property is acquired or construction is completed is called "pre-construction period interest". This interest is NOT deductible

deduction allowable shall be as per clause (B), i.e., ₹30,000 only. Pre-construction interest: Interest paid prior to the year in which the house property is acquired or construction is completed is called "pre-construction period interest". This interest is NOT deductible in the year it is paid. Instead, it is aggregated and allowed as a deduction in 5 equal instalments commencing from the year of completion or acquisition. Each annual instalment is deductible under section 24(b) subject to the overall ceiling. Section 25A — Deduction of unrealised rent: If any portion of arrears of rent is deemed to be income of the previous year under section 25A, then from the amount so deemed, a deduction of thirty per cent (standard deduction) shall be allowed. Section 26 — Co-owners: Where a property belongs to more than one person and their shares are definite and ascertainable, each co-owner shall be assessed in respect of their respective share. Important Conditions for claiming ₹2,00,000 deduction for self-occupied property under section 24(b): 1. Loan must be taken on or after 01-04-1999 for acquisition or construction (not for repair, renewal or reconstruction — those are capped at ₹30,000). 2. Property must be acquired or construction must be completed within 5 years from the end of the financial year in which the loan was taken (i.e., within 5 years from the end of FY in which the EMI started for the first time). 3. Lender's certificate must be obtained certifying the interest amount. Interaction with new tax regime (Section 115BAC): Under the new tax regime (Section 115BAC), the deduction under Section 24(b) is NOT available for self-occupied property. The interest deduction under Section 24(b) is restricted only to let-out properties under the new regime, and only up to the extent of rental income (no loss can be set off under other heads). For old regime: Set-off of house property loss (due to interest in excess of rental income) against other heads is allowed up to ₹2,00,000 per year. The unabsorbed loss can be carried forward for 8 assessment years.

Section 80C — Deduction in respect of life insurance premia, deferred annuity, contributions to provident fund, subscription to certain equity shares or debentures, etc. [IT Act 1961, as amended up to Finance Act 2025] 80C. (1) In computing the total income of an assessee, being an individual or a Hindu undivided family, there shall be deducted, in accordance with and subject to the provisions of this section, the whole of the amount paid or deposited in the previous year, being the aggregate of the sums referred to in sub-section (2), as does not exceed one lakh and fifty thousand rupees. CEILING: ₹1,50,000 per annum (aggregate across all instruments listed in 80C(2)) 80C(2) — Qualifying Investments and Payments: The eligible instruments under Section 80C(2) include: (i) Life Insurance Premium: Premium paid to effect or to keep in force an insurance on the life of the individual assessee, or the spouse or any child of such individual (not more than 10% of the actual capital sum assured; 15% for disabled/critical illness policies). (ii) Deferred annuity: Sum paid to effect or keep in force a contract for a deferred annuity on his own life or the life of his spouse or any child. (iii) Provident Fund contributions: - Public Provident Fund (PPF): Any sum deposited in a PPF account under the PPF Scheme, 1968, or any scheme framed thereunder. Maximum deposit: ₹1,50,000 per year. - Employees' Provident Fund (EPF): Employee's contribution to a Recognised Provident Fund (as defined in rule 67 of Part A of the Fourth Schedule). - Voluntary Provident Fund (VPF): Employee's voluntary contribution over and above the statutory PF contribution. (iv) National Savings Certificate (NSC): Any sum deposited as subscription to National Savings Certificates, VIII Issue (or any other NSC issued under Government Savings Certificates Act, 1959). Accrued interest on NSC is also deemed to be reinvested and qualifies for 80C deduction in subsequent years. (v) ULIP / Pension funds: Sum paid or deposited under UTI Unit Linked Insurance Plan, or eligible pension fund policies. (vi) Home loan repayment (Principal): Any payment made towards the repayment of the amount borrowed

80C deduction in subsequent years. (v) ULIP / Pension funds: Sum paid or deposited under UTI Unit Linked Insurance Plan, or eligible pension fund policies. (vi) Home loan repayment (Principal): Any payment made towards the repayment of the amount borrowed by the assessee from— - Central Government or any State Government - Any bank, including a co-operative bank - Life Insurance Corporation of India - National Housing Bank - Any public company formed and registered in India with the principal object of carrying on the business of providing long-term finance for construction or purchase of houses in India - Any co-operative society engaged in the business of financing the construction of houses for the purpose of purchase or construction of a residential house property, PROVIDED that no deduction under this section shall be allowable in respect of any portion of the repayment which is attributable to interest on such borrowing. Only principal repayment qualifies under 80C — interest is deductible under Section 24(b). (vii) Tuition fees: Any payment made to a university, college, school or other educational institution situated within India, for the purpose of full-time education of any 2 children of the assessee. Only tuition fees are eligible — development fees, donation, capitation fee are not eligible. (viii) Equity Linked Savings Scheme (ELSS): Amount invested in units of an Equity Linked Savings Scheme (ELSS) of a Mutual Fund as notified by the Central Government or as specified under Schedule IV of this Act. Lock-in period: 3 years. (ix) Senior Citizen Savings Scheme (SCSS): Subscription to Senior Citizens Savings Scheme, 2004. Amount at the time of deposit qualifies. (x) Sukanya Samriddhi Account: Amount deposited in Sukanya Samriddhi Account — eligible for 80C deduction. Interest earned and maturity amount are also exempt. (xi) 5-Year Tax Saving Fixed Deposit (FD): A term deposit for not less than 5 years with a scheduled bank with minimum lock-in of 5 years (introduced by Finance (No.2) Act, 2004). (xii) Post Office Time Deposit (5-year): 5-year time deposit under Post Office Time Deposit Rules, 1981. (xiii) Unit Linked Insurance Plans (ULIP): Specified ULIPs from LIC Mutual

bank with minimum lock-in of 5 years (introduced by Finance (No.2) Act, 2004). (xii) Post Office Time Deposit (5-year): 5-year time deposit under Post Office Time Deposit Rules, 1981. (xiii) Unit Linked Insurance Plans (ULIP): Specified ULIPs from LIC Mutual Fund, UTI, etc. 80C(3) — Deduction on premium ratio (for policies issued on or after 01-04-2012): Where the premium payable for any year during the term of the policy exceeds ten per cent of the actual capital sum assured, the amount deductible under this section shall be limited to ten per cent of the actual capital sum assured. 80C(3A) — Persons with disability: Where insurance is on the life of a person with disability or severe disability as referred to in section 80U or suffering from any illness specified in section 80DDB, the premium cap is fifteen per cent (instead of ten per cent) for policies issued on or after 01-04-2013. 80C(5) — Clawback on premature withdrawal: If any amount, in respect of which a deduction is allowed under section 80C, is received back by the assessee— (a) in the case of a life insurance policy, before the end of 5 years from the date of commencement of the insurance; or (b) in other cases, before the expiry of 5 years from the close of the financial year in which the payment was made; then the amount so received (to the extent it was allowed as deduction) shall be deemed to be the income of the assessee in the year of receipt and shall be charged to tax accordingly. For EPF, a similar rule applies if funds are withdrawn before 5 years of continuous service. Important Notes: - Total deduction ceiling under 80C + 80CCC + 80CCD(1) combined = ₹1,50,000 [Section 80CCE] - 80C is NOT available to a company, firm, or AOP/BOI. It is only for individuals and HUFs. - Under the new tax regime (Section 115BAC), deduction under Section 80C is NOT available.

Section 80D — Deduction in respect of health insurance premia and preventive health check-up [IT Act 1961, as amended up to Finance Act 2025] 80D. (1) In computing the total income of an assessee, being an individual or a Hindu undivided family, there shall be deducted such sum, as specified in sub-section (2) or sub-section (3), as the case may be. 80D(2) — For INDIVIDUALS: In the case of an individual being an assessee, the sums referred to in sub-section (1) shall be the following, namely:— (a) the whole of the amount paid to effect or to keep in force an insurance on the health of the assessee or his family (as defined below) or any contribution made to the Central Government Health Scheme or such other scheme as notified by the Central Government in this behalf; or (b) the whole of the amount paid to effect or to keep in force an insurance on the health of the parent or parents of the assessee. Ceiling for 80D(2): - Health insurance premium for self + family (spouse + dependent children): Deduction up to ₹25,000 per annum - If the insured (assessee or spouse) is a senior citizen (aged 60 years or more): Up to ₹50,000 per annum - Preventive health check-up: A deduction of up to ₹5,000 is allowed per family (self + family) from within the above ceilings (not in addition). This ₹5,000 sub-limit may be paid in cash (cash payment is not allowed for insurance premium except for preventive health check-up). Additional deduction for parents: - Premium paid for health insurance of parents: Up to ₹25,000 per annum - If any parent is a senior citizen (aged 60 years or more): Up to ₹50,000 per annum Maximum possible deduction under 80D for an individual: - Own family (non-senior citizens) + Parents (non-senior citizens): ₹25,000 + ₹25,000 = ₹50,000 - Own family (senior citizen assessee or spouse) + Parents (senior citizens): ₹50,000 + ₹50,000 = ₹1,00,000 - Own family (non-senior citizen) + Parents (senior citizens): ₹25,000 + ₹50,000 = ₹75,000 "Family" for 80D purposes means the spouse and dependent

- Own family (senior citizen assessee or spouse) + Parents (senior citizens): ₹50,000 + ₹50,000 = ₹1,00,000 - Own family (non-senior citizen) + Parents (senior citizens): ₹25,000 + ₹50,000 = ₹75,000 "Family" for 80D purposes means the spouse and dependent children of the individual assessee. Uninsured senior citizen parents (without any health insurance policy): Where neither the assessee nor any member of his family or parent has a health insurance policy, but the assessee has incurred medical expenditure in respect of a senior citizen parent (aged 60 years or more), such medical expenditure paid shall be allowed as a deduction of up to ₹50,000 under Section 80D. This covers actual medical expenditure (hospital bills, doctor fees, medicines) for uninsured senior citizen parents. 80D(3) — For HUFs: In the case of a Hindu undivided family, the sums referred to in sub-section (1) shall be the whole of the amount paid to effect or to keep in force an insurance on the health of any member of the HUF. Deduction ceiling: up to ₹25,000 (₹50,000 if insured member is a senior citizen aged 60+). Mode of Payment: Premium must be paid by any mode other than cash. The ₹5,000 sub-limit for preventive health check-up is the only component that can be paid in cash and still be eligible for deduction. Conditions: 1. Premium must be paid by the assessee out of his income chargeable to tax (not from income exempt from tax). 2. The insurance must be with an insurer approved by IRDA (Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India). 3. The insurance policy must be mediclaim/health insurance only (not life insurance). 4. Group insurance paid through employer: If the employer deducts health insurance premium from salary, the employee can claim deduction only for the employee's share; the employer's contribution is a perquisite valued at nil or at actual if applicable. Assessment Year 2025-26 (Budget 2025) — No change to Section 80D limits: Deduction limits under Section 80D remain unchanged for AY 2026-27. The caps of ₹25,000 (non-senior) and ₹50,000 (senior citizen) continue to apply. Availability under tax regimes: Section 80D deduction

Year 2025-26 (Budget 2025) — No change to Section 80D limits: Deduction limits under Section 80D remain unchanged for AY 2026-27. The caps of ₹25,000 (non-senior) and ₹50,000 (senior citizen) continue to apply. Availability under tax regimes: Section 80D deduction is NOT available under the new tax regime (Section 115BAC), unless specifically retained. As per the current law, Section 80D is available ONLY under the old (regular) tax regime. Example for ITR-1: An assessee (age 45) pays ₹18,000 health insurance premium for self + family, ₹45,000 for parents (father 68 years old, mother 63 years old). Preventive check-up ₹3,000. - Self + family: ₹18,000 (within ₹25,000 cap; check-up ₹3,000 included within the cap = total ₹21,000) - Parents (both senior citizens): ₹45,000 (within ₹50,000 cap) - Total 80D deduction: ₹21,000 + ₹45,000 = ₹66,000

Section 80CCD — Deduction in respect of contribution to pension scheme of Central Government (NPS) [IT Act 1961, as amended up to Finance Act 2025] 80CCD(1) — Employee's own contribution to NPS: 80CCD. THIS IS THE KEY PROVISION: Section 80CCD(1B) allows an ADDITIONAL deduction of up to ₹50,000 for NPS contributions, OVER AND ABOVE the ₹1,50,000 ceiling under Section 80CCE. Thus, the effective maximum NPS deduction for an employee

exceed fifty thousand rupees. "Salary" for 80CCD purposes means basic salary plus dearness allowance (DA forming part of salary for retirement benefits). Other allowances are excluded. 80CCD(3) — Clawback on NPS withdrawals: Any amount withdrawn from the NPS account shall be deemed to be the income

Section 80E — Deduction in respect of repayment of loan taken for higher education [IT Act 1961, as amended up to Finance Act 2025] 80E. (1) In computing the total income of an assessee, being an individual, there shall be deducted, in accordance with and subject to the provisions of this section, any amount paid by him in the previous year, out of his income chargeable to tax, by way of payment of interest on loan taken by him from any financial institution or any approved charitable institution for the purpose of pursuing his higher education or for the purpose of higher education of his relative. No upper limit: There is NO ceiling on the amount of deduction — the full interest paid during the year is deductible. What is deductible: ONLY the interest component of the EMI/instalment. Principal repayment is NOT deductible under 80E (unlike home loan principal which qualifies under 80C). Eligible borrowers: The deduction is available only to individuals — not HUFs, companies or other entities. "Higher education" — defined in the Act: "Higher education" means any course of study pursued after passing the Senior Secondary Examination or its equivalent from any school, board or university recognised by the Central Government or State Government or local authority or by any other authority authorised by the Central Government or State Government or local authority to do so. "Relative" — defined in the Act: "Relative" in relation to an individual means the spouse and children of that individual or the student for whom the individual is a legal guardian. This covers the assessee's own education, education of spouse, and education of dependent children (including children for whom the individual is the legal guardian). However, brother's, sister's or parents' education does NOT qualify under section 80E. "Financial institution" — defined in the Act: The loan must be taken from a banking company (including co-operative bank) or any other financial institution notified by the Central Government. Loan from an employer, friend, relative, or private lender does NOT qualify. "Approved charitable institution": Any institution established for charitable purposes and approved by the

banking company (including co-operative bank) or any other financial institution notified by the Central Government. Loan from an employer, friend, relative, or private lender does NOT qualify. "Approved charitable institution": Any institution established for charitable purposes and approved by the prescribed authority under section 10(23C) or section 80G(5)(vi). Duration of deduction: The deduction is available for a MAXIMUM of 8 assessment years (8 years) starting from the year in which the assessee begins to repay the loan, or until the interest is fully repaid, whichever is earlier. If loan repayment extends beyond 8 years, no further 80E deduction is available after the 8th year. Conditions for claiming 80E: 1. Assessee must be an individual. 2. Loan must be taken from an eligible financial institution or approved charitable institution. 3. Loan must be for higher education of self, spouse, or children/legal ward. 4. Deduction is available for interest paid — not principal. 5. No ceiling on deduction amount. 6. Deduction period: Up to 8 assessment years from the year of commencement of repayment. Availability under new tax regime (Section 115BAC): Section 80E deduction for education loan interest is NOT available under the new tax regime. It is exclusively an old (regular) tax regime benefit. Example — ITR-1: An individual paid ₹85,000 as interest on education loan in FY 2024-25 for his daughter's MBA programme. The entire ₹85,000 is deductible under Section 80E (no ceiling applies). This loan was taken in FY 2020-21, so this is the 5th assessment year — deduction is still available for 3 more years after the current year.

Section 80G — Deductions in respect of donations to certain funds, charitable institutions, etc. [IT Act 1961, as amended up to Finance Act 2025] 80G. Overview of Section 80G: Donations to eligible funds and charitable institutions qualify for deduction. The deduction is EITHER 100% or 50% of the donation amount. Additionally, some funds have a 10% of GTI qualifying limit, while others do not. Categories of Donations: Category A — 100% deduction WITHOUT qualifying limit (no 10% GTI cap): - National Defence Fund set up by the Central Government - Prime Minister's National Relief Fund (PMNRF) - PM CARES Fund (PM Citizen Assistance and Relief in Emergency Situations Fund) - National Foundation for Communal Harmony - Chief Minister's Relief Fund (only for states specified) - Lt. Governor's Relief Fund - A University or educational institution of national eminence approved by the prescribed authority - National Blood Transfusion Council or State Blood Transfusion Council - Zila Saksharta Samiti - National/State Children's Fund - National Illness Assistance Fund - Army Central Welfare Fund / Indian Naval Benevolent Fund / Air Force Central Welfare Fund - Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister's Cyclone Relief Fund (and similar disaster relief funds notified by CG) Category B — 50% deduction WITHOUT qualifying limit (no 10% GTI cap): - Jawaharlal Nehru Memorial Fund -

/ Air Force Central Welfare Fund - Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister's Cyclone Relief Fund (and similar disaster relief funds notified by CG) Category B — 50% deduction WITHOUT qualifying limit (no 10% GTI cap): - Jawaharlal Nehru Memorial Fund - Prime Minister's Drought Relief Fund - Indira Gandhi Memorial Trust - Rajiv Gandhi Foundation Category C — 100% deduction WITH 10% of GTI qualifying limit: - Donations to Government or any local authority to be utilised for promoting family planning - Donations made to the Indian Olympic Association or notified sports associations for development of infrastructure for sports Category D — 50% deduction WITH 10% of GTI qualifying limit (most common category): - Any other fund or institution satisfying conditions of section 80G(5), i.e., registered charitable institutions, temples, churches, mosques, etc. - Government or local authority for any charitable purpose other than family planning - Corporations established by Central or State Government for promotion of interest of minority community 10% Qualifying Limit (applies to Categories C and D): The total qualifying amount for donations with the 10% limit shall not exceed 10% of the "Adjusted Gross Total Income" (AGTI), which is: AGTI = Gross Total Income minus long-term capital gains minus short-term capital gains covered under section 111A minus income referred to in sections 115A, 115AB, 115AC, 115AD, 115D minus deductions allowed under any other provisions of Chapter VI-A. For donations to Category D institutions: Deduction = 50% × (amount donated OR 10% of AGTI, whichever is less) Mode of Payment: Effective from AY2018-19: Donations in CASH exceeding ₹2,000 shall NOT be eligible for deduction under Section 80G. Section 80TTA — Deduction in respect of interest on deposits in savings account [IT Act 1961, as amended up to Finance Act 2025] 80TTA. (1) Where the gross total income of an assessee, being an individual or a Hindu undivided family— (a) includes any income by way of interest on deposits (not being time deposits) in a savings account with— (i) a banking company to which the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 applies (including any bank or banking institution referred to in section 51 of that Act); (ii) a co-operative society engaged in carrying on the business of banking (including a co-operative land mortgage bank or a co-operative land development bank); or (iii) a Post Office as defined in clause (k) of section 2 of the Indian Post Office Act, 1898; there shall be allowed, in computing the total income of the assessee, a deduction of an amount equal to the whole of such income or ten thousand rupees, whichever is less. CEILING: ₹10,000 per annum Key definitions and scope: "Deposits" include savings bank account deposits only. Time deposits (Fixed Deposits, Recurring Deposits) are EXCLUDED. Interest from FDs and RDs is fully taxable as Income from Other Sources. "Savings accounts" covered: Regular savings bank accounts in scheduled commercial banks, co-operative banks, or Post Office savings accounts. This includes SB accounts under Post Office Savings Account Scheme. What is NOT covered: - Fixed Deposit (FD) interest — NOT covered by 80TTA - Recurring Deposit (RD) interest — NOT covered by 80TTA - Interest from loans given to friends, relatives — NOT covered - Interest from corporate bonds, debentures, NSC — NOT covered - PPF interest — exempt under Section 10(11), separately Section 80TTB — For Senior Citizens (supersedes 80TTA): Section 80TTB (inserted from AY2019-20) provides a HIGHER deduction to senior citizens (age 60 years or more). Under 80TTB: - Deduction on interest from savings accounts, FDs, RDs, and any deposit with bank, cooperative bank or post office. - Limit: ₹50,000 per annum (vs ₹10,000 under 80TTA) - Senior citizens (60+) should claim 80TTB instead of 80TTA. - 80TTA is NOT available to

from savings accounts, FDs, RDs, and any deposit with bank, cooperative bank or post office. - Limit: ₹50,000 per annum (vs ₹10,000 under 80TTA) - Senior citizens (60+) should claim 80TTB instead of 80TTA. - 80TTA is NOT available to senior citizens who are eligible to claim 80TTB. Interaction between 80TTA and 80TTB: - If the assessee is BELOW 60 years: 80TTA applies (savings account interest only, up to ₹10,000) - If the assessee is 60 YEARS or MORE: 80TTB applies (all interest including FD/RD, up to ₹50,000) - A senior citizen cannot claim BOTH 80TTA and 80TTB simultaneously. Availability under new tax regime (Section 115BAC): Deduction under Section 80TTA is NOT available under the new tax regime. Section 80TTB (senior citizen interest deduction) is also NOT available under the new tax regime. TDS on savings account interest: TDS is NOT deducted on savings bank account interest (banks do not deduct TDS on SB interest). TDS is deducted only on interest from TD (FD/RD) exceeding ₹40,000 per year (₹50,000 for senior citizens). The assessesee must self-declare savings account interest in ITR-1 under "Income from Other Sources" and claim 80TTA deduction. Example for ITR-1: An individual (age 35) earned ₹9,500 as savings account interest from SBI and ₹4,200 from Post Office savings account. Total savings interest = ₹13,700. - Enter ₹13,700 under "Income from Other Sources" in ITR-1. - Claim ₹10,000 as 80TTA deduction (limited to ₹10,000 ceiling). - Net taxable interest from savings = ₹3,700. For a senior citizen (age 65) earning FD interest of ₹38,000 and savings account interest of ₹5,000 = total ₹43,000: - Claim ₹43,000 under IFOS. - 80TTB deduction: ₹43,000 (entire amount, since it is below ₹50,000 cap). - Net taxable interest = NIL.

Section 87A — Rebate of income-tax [IT Act 1961, as amended up to Finance Act 2025] 87A. An assessee, being an individual resident in India, whose total income does not exceed five hundred thousand rupees, shall be entitled to a deduction from the amount of income-tax (before adding Education Cess) on his total income with which he is chargeable under this Act, of an amount equal to hundred per cent of such income-tax or two thousand and five hundred rupees, whichever is less. [PLAIN TEXT: Rebate of ₹12,500 where total taxable income ≤ ₹5,00,000. Applicable under OLD tax regime only at this limit.] OLD REGIME — Section 87A Rebate (AY 2026-27): - Available to: Individual residents only (non-residents, HUFs, companies, etc. are not eligible) - Condition: Total income (after all deductions but before Cess) must NOT exceed ₹5,00,000 - Rebate amount: 100% of income tax or ₹12,500, whichever is LESS - If total income > ₹5,00,000 under old regime: NO rebate NEW REGIME — Section 87A Rebate under Section 115BAC (Budget 2025 amendment): [Finance Act 2025 — applies to income of FY 2025-26, i.e. AY 2026-27] For taxpayers opting for the new tax regime under Section 115BAC(1A): - Available to: Individual residents, HUFs, and eligible assessees opting for 115BAC new regime - Condition: Total income (new regime) must NOT exceed ₹12,00,000 - Rebate amount: 100% of income tax or ₹60,000, whichever is lower (tax at exactly ₹12,00,000 under the new slabs is ₹60,000) - Effective result: Zero income tax for individuals with total income up to ₹12,00,000 under the new regime MARGINAL RELIEF for new regime near ₹12,00,000 threshold: Where total income slightly exceeds ₹12,00,000 (e.g., ₹12,10,000), the tax payable should not exceed the income that exceeds ₹12,00,000. Marginal relief ensures that tax does not exceed the amount by which income exceeds ₹12,00,000. Example marginal relief: If total income = ₹12,50,000 under new regime: - Tax on ₹12,50,000 (new slabs) = ₹20,000 + ₹40,000 + ₹7,500 = ₹67,500 - Marginal relief limits tax to: ₹12,50,000 - ₹12,00,000 = ₹50,000 - Therefore tax payable: ₹50,000 + 4% cess = ₹52,000 -

₹12,50,000 under new regime: - Tax on ₹12,50,000 (new slabs) = ₹20,000 + ₹40,000 + ₹7,500 = ₹67,500 - Marginal relief limits tax to: ₹12,50,000 - ₹12,00,000 = ₹50,000 - Therefore tax payable: ₹50,000 + 4% cess = ₹52,000 - Around ₹12,70,000 the slab tax and the excess become equal; above about ₹12,70,590 the normal slab tax applies. NOTE: The ₹12,00,000 threshold rebate under new regime is specifically enacted through Section 87A as amended for the new regime. The old ₹5,00,000 threshold under Section 87A continues to apply for the old (regular) regime. SPECIAL TAX FOR CAPITAL GAINS (applies to BOTH regimes): Rebate under Section 87A is NOT available against: (i) Tax on Short-Term Capital Gains (STCG) chargeable under Section 111A [taxed at 15% — for equity STCG before 23-07-2024, or 20% for equity STCG after 23-07-2024] (ii) Tax on Long-Term Capital Gains (LTCG) chargeable under Sections 112 and 112A [taxed at special rates] (iii) Tax on special rate income under Section 115BB (lottery, etc.) This restriction means that if the individual's regular income is within the rebate threshold but there are capital gains, the rebate applies only to the regular income tax and NOT to the special-rate capital gains tax. This is a critical planning point: An individual with income of ₹4,00,000 + STCG of ₹2,00,000 under old regime: - Tax on ₹4,00,000 = NIL (within basic exemption of ₹2,50,000 for old regime in slabs) - Tax on STCG ₹2,00,000 @15% = ₹30,000 - Rebate 87A available only on regular income tax — no rebate available on STCG tax since STCG rate is a special rate under 111A. - Total tax = ₹30,000 + cess. ITR-1 applicability: Section 87A rebate is shown as a deduction from tax in ITR-1 Part B TTI (Computation of tax). It is also a key factor in determining whether the individual is in a "zero tax" scenario. "zero tax" scenario. Summary table: Regime | Threshold | Max Rebate | Effective Zero-Tax Limit ----------------|-----------------|----------------|------------------------- Old regime | ₹5,00,000 | ₹12,500 | ₹5,00,000 (with deductions) New regime | ₹12,00,000 | Full tax | ₹12,00,000 (gross income, no deductions needed) Assessment Year 2026-27 specific: The ₹12,00,000 rebate limit for the new regime is effective from AY 2026-27 (FY 2025-26). Section 89A — Relief from taxation in income from retirement benefit account maintained in a notified country [IT Act 1961, as amended up to Finance Act 2025] 89A. Where a specified person has any income of the nature of income from retirement benefit accounts maintained in a notified country, such income shall be taxed in the manner and in the year as may be prescribed. Explanation.— For the purposes of this section— (a) "notified country" means a country notified by the Central Government for the purposes of this section; (b) "retirement benefit account" means an account maintained in the notified country which is similar in nature to the retirement benefit accounts maintained in India (e.g., 401(k), Roth IRA in the USA, similar accounts in Canada, UK); (c) "specified person" means a person who is a citizen of India or a person of Indian origin, and who is or was a resident of a country notified under this section. Background and Purpose: This section was inserted by the Finance Act 2021, effective from Assessment Year 2022-23. Its primary aim is to provide relief to Non-Resident Indians (NRIs) or Persons of Indian Origin (PIOs) who return to India and become tax residents here but have retirement savings in foreign countries (particularly the US, Canada, UK, etc.) maintained in tax-deferred accounts. Without Section 89A: When such a person becomes a resident and ordinarily resident (ROR) in India, the income accruing in their foreign retirement account (e.g., 401(k) growth in the US) becomes taxable in India in the year it accrues, even if no withdrawal is made. This created a double-taxation hardship since the foreign country (e.g., USA) typically taxes such income only at the time of distribution/withdrawal. With Section 89A: The income from the notified foreign retirement account is taxed in India in the year it is received or withdrawn (consistent with how it is taxed in the notified country), not in the year it accrues. This aligns India's taxing point with the foreign country's taxing point, eliminating the mismatch. Notified Countries (as per CBDT notifications): - United States of America (USA) —

it is taxed in the notified country), not in the year it accrues. This aligns India's taxing point with the foreign country's taxing point, eliminating the mismatch. Notified Countries (as per CBDT notifications): - United States of America (USA) — retirement accounts like 401(k), 403(b), Traditional IRA are covered - Canada — retirement accounts like RRSP (Registered Retirement Savings Plan), RRIF are covered - United Kingdom — retirement pension schemes covered (New countries may be notified by CBDT from time to time) Prescribed rules (Rule 21AAA of Income Tax Rules): - Income from notified foreign retirement account that remains in the account (not withdrawn) shall NOT be included in the total income in the year of accrual. - The income shall be included in the total income in the year of withdrawal/distribution from the account. - Where the assessee ceases to be a resident in India before withdrawal, an appropriate method for inclusion and taxation of the accumulated income shall apply. Key points for ITR filing (Form ITR-2, not ITR-1): Section 89A relief is relevant for individuals who: 1. Were non-residents in an earlier period and held foreign retirement accounts 2. Have now become tax residents of India 3. Have income accruing in foreign retirement accounts (interest, capital appreciation, dividends within the account) The relief is primarily relevant for Schedule FSI (Foreign Source Income) and Schedule TR (Tax Relief) in ITR-2. ITR-1 does not accommodate foreign income. Interaction with DTAA: Section 89A works in conjunction with applicable Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement (DTAA) provisions. The applicable DTAA (e.g., India-USA DTAA) may also provide relief; Section 89A provides additional statutory relief where DTAA does not fully address the timing mismatch. Note for ITR-1: ITR-1 (Sahaj) is not applicable for persons with foreign income. Individuals with Section 89A income must file ITR-2. This section is documented here for completeness of the knowledge base.

Form 16 is a certificate issued by an employer to an employee under Section 203 of the Income Tax Act, 1961. It certifies the amount of TDS (Tax Deducted at Source) deducted from the employee's salary and deposited with the Central Government on behalf of the employee. It also serves as a comprehensive income and deduction summary for the financial year. Form 16 consists of TWO PARTS: - Part A: TDS summary (certificates of tax deducted and deposited, generated from TRACES portal) - Part B: Salary and deduction details (annexure prepared by employer) FORM 16 — PART A: Part A is generated by the employer from the TRACES (TDS Reconciliation Analysis and Correction Enabling System) portal. FORM 12B: When an employee joins a new employer mid-year, they must submit Form 12B to the new employer declaring income and TDS from previous employer. This enables the new employer to deduct TDS on aggregate income. Failure to submit may result in lower TDS by the new employer and a self-assessment tax demand at the time of ITR filing. FORM 16A: Form 16A is a TDS certificate for non-salary income (FD interest, professional fees, rent, etc.). It is different from Form 16 (which is exclusively for salary).
